q: Is there a one-query variant of the paper's Lemma 1 (amplitude-encoding of a unit-modulus function) that removes the 1/q Lemma-1 penalty and lifts the total finite-field hidden-shift success probability from (1-1/q)^2 to at least (1-1/q)?
basis: Our exact statevector on F_13 hit peak probability 0.923 conditional on Lemma-1 success, exactly matching (1-1/p). The paper's (1-1/p)^2 headline number is entirely attributable to the Lemma-1 amplitude-construction failure branch, not to the QFT-diagonalisation step. That branch uses 2 oracle queries; amplitude amplification across those 2 queries plausibly boosts the amplitude-construction success probability closer to 1.
next_steps: Implement a Grover-style amplitude amplifier around the 2-query Lemma-1 sub-circuit and measure the composite success probability at p = 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. If it exceeds (1-1/p)^2 empirically, formalise the analysis and see whether the trick generalises to arbitrary finite fields F_q with the multiplicative-character oracle.

q: For Boolean g on Z_N with non-flat but nowhere-zero Fourier spectrum, which combinatorial invariant of g tightly bounds the hidden-shift-algorithm peak measurement probability -- is it min_y |g_hat(y)|^2, the flatness ratio max/min, or a higher moment?
basis: Our Boolean-g runs on Z_8, Z_16, Z_32 gave peak probabilities 0.729, 0.699, 0.804 respectively; the min|g_hat| values were 0.293, 0.207, 0.354, roughly tracking the peak-prob ordering but not proportional to any obvious invariant we computed. A tight closed-form bound would let cryptographic reductions choose oracle functions with certified quantum-attack success probability.
next_steps: Sweep a large ensemble of random Boolean g on Z_N for N in {8, 16, 32, 64}, compute the exact peak probability of the paper's algorithm along with (i) min|g_hat|, (ii) sum |1/g_hat|^2, (iii) L^4 norm of g_hat, and regress; then attempt an analytical proof that the best predictor is a lower bound.

q: Does replacing the paper's multiplicative-character oracle by a Zadoff-Chu chirp g(x)=exp(2 pi i a x^2 / 2N) preserve the cryptographic implications (attacks on algebraically homomorphic schemes), or does the field structure of F_p do essential work beyond just providing a flat-spectrum g?
basis: We used a chirp as the flat-spectrum stand-in on Z_N and it recovered s deterministically -- exactly like the paper's Legendre case on F_p. If the cryptographic attack only needs a known flat-spectrum g, chirps might extend the paper's Section 4 attack framework to composite-modulus rings that lack quadratic characters.
next_steps: Rewrite the Section 4 cryptographic reduction (attacking Boneh-Lipton's algebraically homomorphic cryptosystem) with 'multiplicative character' replaced by 'known flat-spectrum function'; check whether the security reduction still goes through, or whether it uses the multiplicativity chi(xy)=chi(x)chi(y) in an essential way beyond spectrum flatness.

q: Can the empirical peak-probability curve of the shifted-Legendre-symbol algorithm on small primes numerically test or refine Conjecture 2.1 of Boneh-Lipton (needed for the dihedral-HSP reduction in the paper)?
basis: Our exact simulation on p=13 gives the full |psi|^2 distribution after the algorithm's inverse QFT, including the residual amplitudes on wrong shifts. The paper reduces to dihedral HSP only under Conjecture 2.1; the residual-amplitude pattern predicted by (or violating) the conjecture should be directly observable in our simulation data.
next_steps: Extend our Legendre code to p in {7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31}, dump the full post-measurement distribution, and fit it against the pattern the conjecture predicts. Publish the tables in an appendix and see if the conjecture-consistent residuals are visible.

q: For the paper's Section 5.2 unknown-n variant (using approximate Fourier sampling with m = Omega(n^2/eps^2), q = Omega(m/eps)), what is the smallest polylogarithmic sample size that still recovers s with constant probability, in practice?
basis: We did NOT implement the unknown-n case (out of wave-time scope); the paper only gives asymptotics. The literature does not appear to have a plot of empirical success probability vs (n, eps, m, q). A quantitative curve would show whether the approximation constants are practical or hopeless at moderate n.
next_steps: Implement the approximate-Fourier-sampling wrapper around our known-N algorithm; run at n in {16, 32, 64, 128} with m/n^2 sweeping in {0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8} and eps in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}; report success probability as a heatmap; identify the smallest (m, q) that still hits >= 0.5 success and compare to the theoretical Omega(n^2/eps^2).
